content: The effectiveness of oral stimulation interventions in achieving oral feeding in preterm infants born before 37 weeks of postmenstrual age was evaluated. The study selection criteria included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing defined oral stimulation interventions with no intervention, standard care, sham treatment, or non-oral interventions. A total of 19 trials involving 823 participants from countries such as Brazil, China, France, India, Iran, the United Kingdom, and the United States were included. A systematic review was conducted to assess the avoidance of bottles and artificial teats during the establishment of breastfeeding in healthy term infants. The focus was on the impact of avoiding bottle feeds on successful breastfeeding. The study selection criteria included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials. Two trials with 1241 participants from Switzerland and the United States were included. The effects of cup feeding versus other forms of enteral feeding on weight gain and successful breastfeeding in term and preterm infants unable to fully breastfeed were examined. The study selection criteria included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing cup feeding to other enteral feeding methods. Five trials with 971 participants from Australia, Brazil, Turkey, the United Kingdom, and the United States were included. The impact of avoiding bottle feeds during the establishment of breastfeeding in preterm infants on the likelihood of successful breastfeeding and the safety of alternatives to bottle feeds was reviewed. The study selection criteria included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing the avoidance of bottles with the use of bottles in women who chose to breastfeed their preterm infants. Seven trials with 1152 participants from Australia, Brazil, Turkey, the United Kingdom, and the United States were included. The role of hospitals with written breastfeeding policy statements in implementing the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding and improving breastfeeding rates and duration was assessed. The study selection criteria included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials, non-randomized trials, and observational studies. One study with 916 infants from Brazil was included. The effectiveness of education and training programs for healthcare staff in improving their knowledge, attitudes, and skills to support breastfeeding women was evaluated. The study selection criteria included randomized controlled trials comparing breastfeeding education and training for health workers with no or usual training. Three trials with 250 participants from Brazil, Denmark, and Sweden were included. The impact of antenatal breastfeeding education on increasing the initiation and duration of breastfeeding was assessed. The study selection criteria included randomized controlled trials evaluating formal antenatal breastfeeding education or comparing different methods of antenatal breastfeeding education. Twenty-four trials with 10,056 women from Australia, Canada, China, Denmark, Singapore, the United Kingdom, and the United States were included. The effectiveness of interventions promoting the initiation of breastfeeding was evaluated. The study selection criteria included randomized controlled trials of any breastfeeding-promotion intervention in any population group. Twenty-eight trials with 107,362 women from Ghana, Malawi, Nicaragua, Nigeria, the United Kingdom, and the United States were included. The importance of providing linkage to breastfeeding support groups after discharge to improve breastfeeding outcomes was examined. The study selection criteria included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials reporting on providing information on linkage to breastfeeding support for women at discharge compared to no linkage. Two cluster randomized controlled trials with 5590 mother–infant pairs from Australia and the Democratic Republic of Congo were included. GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations) was used to assess the quality of evidence. High-quality evidence indicates high confidence that the true effect is close to the estimate. Moderate-quality evidence suggests the true effect is likely close to the estimate but may differ. Low-quality evidence indicates limited confidence, and the true effect may differ substantially. Very low-quality evidence reflects very little confidence, with the true effect likely differing substantially.
